data.title: Check-ups and cleanings
data.summary: A full exam, a gentle clean and a plain-English rundown of what we saw. Every six months for most people.

$media.alt: A dentist showing a patient how to angle a toothbrush along the gum line.

data.price: $185 without insurance. Usually covered in full by PPO plans.

steps.title: Talk first
steps.body: We ask what has changed since last time and whether anything hurts. You stay sitting up for this part.

steps.title: Exam and x-rays
steps.body: A check of every tooth and your gums, plus low-dose digital x-rays once a year.

steps.title: Clean and polish
steps.body: Our hygienist removes build-up by hand, then polishes. Tell us if anything feels sharp and we slow down.

steps.title: Your plan
steps.body: You leave with what we found, what can wait, and what anything would cost. Written down.

faqs.q: How often should I come in?
faqs.a: Every six months suits most adults and kids. If your gums need closer watching we may suggest every three or four months, and we will explain why.
Most PPO plans cover two check-ups a year in full. June checks your plan before your visit and tells you if anything is not covered.

faqs.q: Do I have to have x-rays?
faqs.a: No. We recommend them once a year because they show problems between teeth that we cannot see. You can always say no.

children.text: A check-up at Linden takes an hour, which is longer than most practices book. That extra time is where the explaining happens.
We do not lecture. If we spot something, we show you on the screen, tell you whether it needs doing now or can be watched, and give you the price before anything is scheduled.

data.title: Clear aligners
data.summary: Straighter teeth without metal braces, planned on a 3D scan, with check-ins every six to eight weeks.

$media.alt: A hand lifting a clear aligner out of its open case.

data.price: $3,900 to $5,400 depending on the case. Monthly payment plans available.

steps.title: Scan and preview
steps.body: A 3D scan, no goopy moulds, and a preview of how your teeth should move.

steps.title: Fit your first set
steps.body: We fit the first aligners and show you how to put them in and take them out.

steps.title: Check in
steps.body: A short visit every six to eight weeks to make sure things are on track.

steps.title: Keep it straight
steps.body: A retainer at the end, so the result lasts.

faqs.q: Am I a good fit for aligners?
faqs.a: Most mild to moderate crowding and gaps can be treated with aligners. A free consult and scan will tell us for sure.

faqs.q: How many hours a day do I wear them?
faqs.a: About 22. You take them out to eat and to brush.

children.text: Aligners work well for most adults and older teens with mild to moderate crowding. We start with a free consult and scan, and we will tell you if braces would do a better job.

data.title: Emergency care
data.summary: Toothache, a chipped tooth or a lost filling. We keep slots open every weekday for same-day and next-day visits.

$media.alt: A dentist holding up a patient's x-ray and pointing out the problem tooth.

data.price: $95 for the emergency exam and x-ray. Treatment priced on the day.

steps.title: Call before 10 am
steps.body: Ring us and June will find you a slot, usually the same day.

steps.title: Find the cause
steps.body: An exam and a single x-ray to see what is going on.

steps.title: Stop the pain
steps.body: We treat the pain first. Longer work can be booked once you are comfortable.

faqs.a: Pain that keeps you up at night, swelling, a broken or knocked-out tooth, or a lost crown. If you are not sure, call and ask.

faqs.q: What if it is after hours?
faqs.a: Our voicemail has an on-call number for current patients. For facial swelling that affects breathing or swallowing, go to the ER.

faqs.q: I knocked a tooth out. What do I do?
faqs.a: Pick it up by the crown, not the root, rinse it briefly, and keep it in milk. Call us straight away. The first hour matters most.

children.text: Tooth pain does not wait for your next check-up. We hold back a few appointments every weekday so we can see people the same day they call.
You do not need to be a current patient. Call, tell June what happened, and we will tell you what it is likely to cost before you come in.

data.title: Fillings and crowns
data.summary: Tooth-coloured fillings and same-week crowns, explained on screen first, priced before we start.

$media.alt: A dentist walking a patient through her x-rays on a tablet before treatment.

data.price: Fillings $190 to $310. Crowns from $1,150. Insurance usually pays half or more.

steps.title: See it first
steps.body: We show you the tooth on screen and explain what a filling or crown would fix.

steps.title: Price in writing
steps.body: You get the cost, and what your insurance should cover, before you book.

steps.title: Numb, then wait
steps.body: We check the area is fully numb before we start. If it is not, we wait or top up.

steps.title: Check the bite
steps.body: We adjust until your bite feels normal, then send you off with aftercare notes.

faqs.a: No. We use tooth-coloured composite for fillings. It bonds to the tooth and matches its shade.

faqs.q: How long does a crown take?
faqs.a: Two visits about a week apart. The first shapes the tooth and fits a temporary crown, the second fits the permanent one.

children.text: Nobody books a filling for fun. Our job is to make it quick, properly numb, and free of surprises on the bill.
Marcus does most of our restorative work and talks you through every step as he goes. Patients say it helps to know what the noises are.

data.title: Kids’ dentistry
data.summary: First visits from age one, check-ups that feel like a game, and sealants that stop most cavities before they start.

$media.alt: A young girl smiling up at a dentist from the chair while her mother sits beside her.

data.price: $120 for a check-up under age 12. Covered by most plans and Oregon Health Plan.

steps.title: Meet the chair
steps.body: Kids get a ride up and down in the chair and a look at the tools before anything goes in their mouth.

steps.title: Count the teeth
steps.body: A quick look with a mirror, counted out loud. Many first visits stop here, and that is fine.

steps.title: A quick clean
steps.body: A soft polish and fluoride if they are happy to keep going.

steps.title: Parent debrief
steps.body: Five minutes with you on brushing, snacks and what to watch for next.

faqs.q: When should my child first see a dentist?
faqs.a: Around their first birthday, or six months after the first tooth comes in. Early visits are mostly about getting used to the place.

faqs.q: Can I stay in the room?
faqs.a: Yes. Most parents sit right next to the chair. Some older kids prefer you in the waiting room, and we follow their lead.
A thin coating painted onto the back teeth to keep food out of the grooves. It takes a few minutes per tooth and does not involve any drilling.

children.text: Most adults who dread the dentist can trace it back to one bad visit as a kid. We try hard to make sure that visit never happens here.
First visits go at your child’s pace. If all they do is ride the chair and count their teeth, that counts as a good visit, and we book the next one.

data.title: Nervous patients
data.summary: Longer appointments, a stop signal you control, and the option of nitrous oxide. No judgement about how long it has been.

$media.alt: A young woman laughing with the dentist during her appointment.

data.price: No extra charge for longer slots. Nitrous oxide is $75 per visit.

steps.title: Tell us on the form
steps.body: Tick the box when you book. We will not ask you to explain unless you want to.

steps.title: A talk-only first visit
steps.body: Your first appointment can be just a conversation in our consult room, away from the chair.

steps.title: Agree a stop signal
steps.body: Raise your left hand and we stop, every time, no questions.

steps.title: Go at your pace
steps.body: We split treatment across shorter visits if that is easier.

faqs.q: It has been years since I saw a dentist. Will I get a lecture?
faqs.a: No. A lot of our patients come to us after five or ten years away. We start from where you are today.
We offer nitrous oxide (laughing gas), which wears off in minutes so you can drive home. For deeper sedation we refer to a specialist we trust.

faqs.q: Can I bring someone with me?
faqs.a: Yes. A friend or partner is welcome in the room.

children.text: If you feel anxious about the dentist, you are in good company. About a third of our patients tell us so on their first form.
We book you double time, explain each step before it happens, and stop the moment you raise your hand. You are in charge of the pace.

data.title: Whitening
data.summary: Custom take-home trays that whiten safely over two weeks, with less sensitivity than the shop-bought kind.

$media.alt: A woman in the dental chair smiling at her teeth in a hand mirror.

data.price: $350 for custom trays and gel. Top-up gel $40.

steps.title: Check first
steps.body: We make sure there is no decay or gum problem that whitening would aggravate.

steps.title: Fit your trays
steps.body: Trays made from a scan of your teeth, so the gel stays where it should.

steps.title: Two weeks at home
steps.body: About 30 minutes a day. Most people see the change within the first week.

faqs.a: Some people feel mild sensitivity for a day or two. Custom trays and a lower-strength gel keep it to a minimum.

faqs.q: Will it whiten my crowns or fillings?
faqs.a: No. Whitening only works on natural enamel. We will tell you at your check if that affects your result.

children.text: Whitening is optional and we will never push it. If you want it, custom trays are the safest way to do it at home, and the trays last for years of top-ups.

data.title: The two-minute rule, and brushing habits that stick
data.excerpt: Small changes that get kids, and their parents, brushing properly without a nightly fight.
data.author: $ref:team-marcus-oyelaran

$media.alt: Two children brushing their teeth together at a sunny bathroom sink.

children.text: Most people brush for about 45 seconds. Two minutes feels long until you time it, and then it feels very long.
Use a timer you do not have to watch
A two-minute song works better than a sand timer. Electric brushes with a 30-second buzz are even better, because they also tell you when to move to the next quarter of your mouth.
Brush together
Kids copy. If they see you brush at the same time, they brush longer. It also means you can check their back teeth, which is where most kids’ cavities show up.
Keep the brush where they can see it
Out of sight is out of mind. A cup by the sink, at their height, does a surprising amount of the work.
Do not rinse after
Spit, do not rinse. Rinsing washes away the fluoride that keeps working after you stop brushing. It is the easiest change on this list.

data.title: What a check-up costs in Portland without insurance
data.excerpt: Our prices, why they vary between practices, and how our membership plan works.
data.author: $ref:team-june-halvorsen

$media.alt: A patient checking in at a wooden reception desk with a smiling coordinator.

children.text: People call us every week asking this, often a little embarrassed to ask. You should not be. A price you can plan for is part of good care.
Our prices
A new-patient exam, x-rays and cleaning is $185 at Linden. A returning check-up and clean is $165. Kids under 12 are $120. Those are the full prices, with nothing added at the desk.
Why prices vary

Across Portland you will see anything from about $150 to $400 for the same visit. The difference usually comes down to which x-rays are included, whether the cleaning is billed separately, and how long the appointment is. Ask any practice for the total, including x-rays, before you book.
The membership plan

If you do not have insurance, our membership costs $29 a month for adults and $19 for kids. It covers two check-ups and cleanings a year, all routine x-rays, one emergency exam, and 15 percent off any treatment. Most members save money in the first year.
What we promise
You will always get the price before treatment, in writing. If something changes partway through, we stop and tell you.

data.title: Do you need to floss?
data.excerpt: A straight answer, and what to do instead if you know you will never floss.
data.author: $ref:team-ana-whitlock

$media.alt: Three wooden toothbrushes standing in a white cup next to a sprig of greenery.

children.text: Short answer: you need to clean between your teeth. Floss is one way to do it, and for a lot of people it is not the best one.
Why between the teeth matters
Your toothbrush cleans about 60 percent of each tooth’s surface. The rest is the sides, where teeth touch. That is where most adult cavities and nearly all gum disease start.
If you hate flossing

Try interdental brushes. They are tiny bottle brushes that slide between teeth, and most patients find them faster and easier than floss. We will show you which sizes fit your gaps at your next check-up.
Water flossers are another option, especially if you have braces, bridges or implants. They are less thorough than brushes but far better than nothing.
How often
Once a day, any time. Before bed is ideal, but the best time is whichever one you will stick to.
What we will not do
Lecture you about it. If you are not cleaning between your teeth now, starting with three nights a week is a real improvement, and we will notice it at your next visit.

data.title: Getting a nervous kid through their first check-up
data.excerpt: What we tell parents the week before, what to say in the car, and the one word to avoid.
data.author: $ref:team-danielle-okafor

$media.alt: A young girl in the dental chair grinning at her teeth in a hand mirror.

children.text: I see three or four first visits a week. The kids who do best are not the bravest ones. They are the ones whose parents kept it boring.
The week before

Read a picture book about the dentist together, once or twice. Let them brush a stuffed animal’s teeth. That is enough preparation. More than that and the visit starts to feel like a big deal, which is the opposite of what you want.
In the car

Keep it short and true. “We’re going to count your teeth and see the chair that goes up and down.” Kids handle plain facts far better than reassurance. If you say “it won’t hurt”, the first thing they hear is the word hurt.
The word to avoid
Shot. Also needle, drill and pull. We have our own words for the tools, like the tooth counter and the water squirt, and we would love you to leave the explaining to us.
When it does not go to plan

Some kids cry. Some refuse to open their mouth. We have seen it all, and it is fine. A visit where your child sits in the chair, holds the mirror and goes home is still a good first visit. We will book a short follow-up and try again.
After
Make a fuss of it, but not with sweets. A trip to the park or picking the dinner works well. Next time, they will remember the park.

story.paragraph: Ana spent nine years in a downtown group practice where every check-up was booked into fifteen minutes. She liked the people. She did not like watching patients leave confused about what had just happened in their own mouths.
In 2016 she took over a tired single-chair surgery on SE Tacoma Street, knocked through to the empty shop next door, and opened Linden with a simple rule: book less, explain more.
Ten years on, most new patients find us through a neighbour. A lot of them have not seen a dentist in years. We think that says more about how dentistry is usually delivered than about them.

motion_items.name: Line reveals
motion_items.why: Gives each section heading a clear arrival without moving body text.
motion_items.how: GSAP SplitText lines in a mask, once, on enter.

motion_items.name: Manifesto fill
motion_items.why: Reads the core promise at the visitor's pace.
motion_items.how: Words go from 16% to 100% opacity, scrubbed to scroll.

motion_items.name: First-visit pan
motion_items.why: Tells the appointment as a sequence, which is what nervous patients want to know.
motion_items.how: Section pins at the top; vertical scroll moves the track sideways. Swipeable list on touch screens.

motion_items.name: Service preview
motion_items.why: Puts a face to each service without adding images to the list.
motion_items.how: A photo follows the cursor and swaps per row. Fine pointers only.

motion_items.name: Parallax frames
motion_items.why: Adds depth to framed photos so the calm layout does not feel flat.
motion_items.how: Image drifts within its frame, about 5 to 8 percent.

motion_items.name: Reading progress
motion_items.why: Shows how much of a journal post is left.
motion_items.how: A 3px bar under the nav, scrubbed to the article.

data.inspiration_intro: UK and US studios only. We studied each one and took a single idea from it.

inspiration_items.title: Dental Website, Confidence Before the Appointment
inspiration_items.took: Warm off-white base and a small card sitting on the hero photo. Ours carries opening hours instead of a booking widget.

inspiration_items.title: Bloom, mental health clinic
inspiration_items.took: The inset, rounded photo frame. It became the hero reveal: the frame opens out from an inset clip.

inspiration_items.title: Atelier Aesthetica, aesthetic clinic
inspiration_items.took: Calm pacing, generous margins and short, declarative headlines.

inspiration_items.title: Website and motion concept for a dentist clinic
inspiration_items.took: Real, diverse faces and motion that feels playful without being loud. The cursor-follow photo on the services list comes from here.

inspiration_items.title: Women's hormone clinic
inspiration_items.took: A single reassuring sentence given the whole screen. That is our scroll-filled manifesto.

inspiration_items.title: Dental clinic landing page
inspiration_items.took: Big confident type set against photography, and process explained as a sequence of image cards.

inspiration_items.title: Nova Dental, team page
inspiration_items.took: Large portraits with a human detail beside each one, which shaped our team bios.
